newsitem.title: JAPAN: Sumitomo's Hamanaka faces more legal trouble.
newsitem.headline: Sumitomo's Hamanaka faces more legal trouble.

text.p: Former star copper trader Yasuo Hamanaka was indicted on forgery charges on Tuesday, while his former employer Sumitomo Corp accused him of committing fraud in connection with a $2.6 billion trading scandal.

Sumitomo alleged that Hamanaka committed fraud through a newly disclosed Hong Kong connection. Tokyo prosecutors then issued formal indictments against Hamanaka on four counts of forgery, the crime for which he was arrested three weeks ago.
Under Japanese law, a conviction on the fraud charges would be much more serious than a forgery conviction.

Hamanaka was the most controversial and influential figure in the world copper market until he was sacked in June for allegedly racking up $2.6 billion in losses from his apparently unauthorised trades.
The losses are the biggest in financial history.
A source close to the Tokyo prosecutors office said Hamanaka would be served with an arrest warrant for fraud on Wednesday, following Sumitomo's filing on Tuesday of the formal fraud complaint.
The filing of such a complaint kicks off the legal process against an individual.

Hamanaka's arrest on October 22, on suspicion of forgery, came one day after Sumitomo filed a complaint with Tokyo prosecutors alleging he forged two documents in 1994 authorising him to engage in certain copper transactions.
Tuesday's indictment included two additional charges that he forged a managing director's name in 1993.

One of Hamanaka's lawyers said the ex-trader could be sentenced for up to 10 years if he is convicted of the fraud alleged in Tuesday's complaint by Sumitomo. A forgery conviction could result in a sentence of up to five years.

Sumitomo's latest complaint states that in 1994 Hamanaka fraudulently raised $770 million through a Hong Kong subsidiary of Sumitomo, under the false pretext of purchasing copper warrants, in order to cover losses from unauthorised futures deals.
Sumitomo said the funds were later repaid to the Hong Kong unit with profits from other off-the-books derivatives trades and that all of the transactions were hidden from the company.

Sumitomo has alleged that Hamanaka incurred a loss of 6.5 billion yen ($58 million) from unauthorised trading in 1985, while subsequent secret deals attempting to erase the losses simply compounded them until they snowballed into a multi-billion-dollar catastrophe.
Sumitomo also said it was in discussions with Tokyo prosecutors about a possible complaint against Hamanaka for breach of trust.

Following Hamanaka's arrest last month, his lawyer said the former copper trader had admitted to committing forgery, although he denied that he manipulated the world copper market or acted for personal gain. ($1=112 yen)
